content: Rice fortification with vitamins and minerals has the potential to address micronutrient deficiencies in populations that rely heavily on rice as a staple food. Globally, approximately 490 million metric tonnes of rice are consumed annually, serving as the primary food source for around three billion people. This intervention aims to improve micronutrient status and health outcomes by adding nutrients such as iron, vitamin A, zinc, or folic acid to rice. To evaluate the effects of rice fortification, researchers conducted a systematic review of studies, including randomized controlled trials (RCTs), quasi-randomized trials, and controlled before-and-after studies. The participants were individuals older than two years, including pregnant women, from various countries. The intervention involved rice fortified with at least one micronutrient or a combination of several, compared to unfortified rice or no intervention. Seventeen studies involving 10,483 participants were included in the review, with two additional studies ongoing. Twelve of these were RCTs, and five were non-randomized studies. The studies were conducted in countries such as India, Thailand, the Philippines, Brazil, Bangladesh, Burundi, Cambodia, Indonesia, Mexico, and the USA. The participants included non-pregnant, non-lactating women and children of preschool or school age. All studies involved rice fortified with iron, either alone or in combination with other micronutrients like zinc, vitamin A, or folic acid. The amount of elemental iron in the fortified rice ranged from 0.2 to 112.8 mg per 100 g of uncooked rice, with intervention durations varying from two weeks to 48 months. The methodological quality of the studies varied. Thirteen studies did not clearly describe their methods for sequence generation or allocation concealment. Eleven studies had a low attrition rate, and there was no evidence of selective reporting. However, most studies had a high or unclear risk of bias in several domains. The funding sources for the studies included government, private, and non-governmental organizations, as well as academic institutions, and there was no indication that funding influenced the results. The findings of the review are as follows: 1. Iron Fortification: Fortification of rice with iron alone or in combination with other micronutrients may have little or no effect on reducing the risk of anemia (risk ratio [RR] 0.72, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.54 to 0.97; low-certainty evidence). It may reduce the risk of iron deficiency (RR 0.66, 95% CI 0.51 to 0.84; low-certainty evidence). Fortified rice may increase mean hemoglobin levels slightly (mean difference [MD] 1.83 g/L, 95% CI 0.66 to 3.00; low-certainty evidence). There may be little or no effect on vitamin A deficiency when vitamin A is included in the fortification (RR 0.68, 95% CI 0.36 to 1.29; low-certainty evidence). One study suggested that rice fortified with folic acid may improve serum or plasma folate levels (MD 4.30 nmol/L, 95% CI 2.00 to 6.60; low-certainty evidence). Another study indicated that rice fortified with iron alone or in combination with other micronutrients may slightly increase the risk of hookworm infection (RR 1.78, 95% CI 1.18 to 2.70; low-certainty evidence). The effect of fortified rice on diarrhea is uncertain (RR 3.52, 95% CI 0.18 to 67.39; very low-certainty evidence). 2. Vitamin A Fortification: One study examined rice fortified with vitamin A alone and found that it may increase mean hemoglobin levels (MD 10.00 g/L, 95% CI 8.79 to 11.21; low-certainty evidence). It may also slightly improve serum retinol concentrations (MD 0.17 µmol/L, 95% CI 0.13 to 0.21; low-certainty evidence). 3. Folic Acid and Zinc Fortification: Studies involving folic acid and zinc also included iron in the fortification arms, and their effects were reported as part of the findings for iron fortification. The authors concluded that fortification of rice with iron alone or in combination with other micronutrients may have limited effects on reducing anemia or iron deficiency and may slightly increase hemoglobin levels in the general population older than two years. Fortification with vitamin A or folic acid may have little or no effect on vitamin A deficiency or serum folate concentrations. There is limited evidence regarding potential adverse effects of rice fortification.
